\clearpage

% ===================================================================== %
\section{Secondary ionization in a molecular gas: the H$_2$ target the
prescription never had, the heating fraction that went to zero in a neutral
gas, and the two heat returns that were blocked on unsourced constants
(2026-09-02)}\label{sec:sec-ion-molecular}
% ===================================================================== %

\textbf{The judgement first.} EXHALE's photoelectron partition is the
Shull \& van Steenberg (1985, ApJ 298, 268) prescription, and \textbf{it has
no H$_2$ term in either direction}: molecular hydrogen was a source of
photoelectrons in \texttt{PH\_heat\_HHe} but never a target, so in a layer
where 92\% of the hydrogen nuclei are bound into H$_2$ the energy that should
ionize H$_2$ was handed to H\,\textsc{i}, and the heat that comes back when a
photoelectron dissociates H$_2$ was not returned at all. The routine's own
docstring said so. That is missing physics, not a missing option.

Repairing it turned up three more defects in the same prescription, and this
section records all four: the missing H$_2$ target, a heating fraction
evaluated eight to twelve decades outside the range its authors state (and
going to \emph{zero} where the true value is $0.11$--$0.26$), ionization
channels applied without the energy axis their sources say they need, and an
``ionized fraction'' that was a count of H and He ions rather than the
electron density both sources define. Each was built and measured on its own
build, because all four move the same integral.

The source is Dalgarno, Yan \& Liu (1999, ApJS 125, 237), \emph{Electron
Energy Deposition in a Gas Mixture of Atomic and Molecular Hydrogen and
Helium}. Every coefficient below was read from the published paper, and the
two tables the change stands on (their Tables 5 and 7) and their equations
(9) and (10) were checked against the \emph{rendered pages} rather than a
text extraction, because the extraction of this paper turns \texttt{+} and
\texttt{x} into the same character: their eq.~(17) reads
$a(x) = 0.5 + (x/10^4)^{0.15}$ in the extracted text and
$a(x) = 0.5 \times (x/10^4)^{0.15}$ on the page.

\subsection*{What was missing, and how large it is}

Three separate defects, of which this section repairs the first.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{No H$_2$ ionization channel.} The hydrogenic share of the
  secondary ionization energy went entirely to H\,\textsc{i}.
\item \textbf{No molecular heat return.} A photoelectron in H$_2$ loses
  energy to rotational excitation, to dissociation through the triplet
  states, to vibrational excitation and to the Lyman and Werner bands. In a
  gas dense enough to quench the internal excitation most of that comes back
  as heat. None of it was carried.
\item \textbf{The heating amplitude is evaluated far outside its own stated
  range.} Shull \& van Steenberg state their fits for $0.0001 < x < 1.0$ ---
  ``the fit to the heating curve, which is reproduced to $\sim$2\% over the
  range $0.0001 < x < 1.0$'' --- and their heating form goes to \emph{zero}
  as $x \rightarrow 0$. Our molecular layer sits at $x = 10^{-16}$ to
  $5\times10^{-5}$, up to twelve decades below the range they state, and the
  true heating fraction of a neutral gas is not zero but $0.11$--$0.26$
  (Dalgarno et al.\ Table 7; Shull \& van Steenberg's own Monte Carlo gives
  $0.1358 \pm 0.0088$ at their lowest $x = 10^{-4}$, against $0.1114$ for
  their fit there). Repairing that amplitude moves every run, molecular or
  not, and is deliberately \emph{not} in this section.
\end{enumerate}

The size is best given as a property of the prescription evaluated on a
composition, not as the movement of an answer --- the molecular gates are
fixed-step relaxation snapshots and their movement is admissible only as a
bit-identity test. Taking the composition of \texttt{mol\_base\_handoff} and
a 100~eV photoelectron:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
 & at the base & mid-layer & top of the layer \\
\midrule
$n(\mathrm{H_2})/n(\mathrm{H\,I})$ & 6.2 & 31 & 0.011 \\
before                                      & 0.0015 & 0.0105 & 0.0910 \\
after this change                           & \textbf{0.0720} & \textbf{0.0812} & \textbf{0.0916} \\
with defects 2 and 3 also repaired          & 0.259 & 0.268 & 0.164 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

so this change carries about a third of the total and the two deferred
repairs carry the rest. The last column is a cell with almost no H$_2$ left,
where the whole remaining difference is defect (3).

\subsection*{One collision weight in place of two mean energies}

Dalgarno et al.\ give the three-species mixture as two separate statements,
their eqs.\ (9) and (10),
%
\begin{equation*}
  W_m(\mathrm{H^+}) = W_q(\mathrm{H^+})
     \left[1 + 1.89\,\frac{n(\mathrm{H_2})}{n(\mathrm{H})}\right],
  \qquad
  W_m(\mathrm{H_2^+}) = W_q(\mathrm{H_2^+})
     \left[1 + 0.53\,\frac{n(\mathrm{H})}{n(\mathrm{H_2})}\right] .
\end{equation*}
%
\textbf{The product of the two coefficients is
$1.89 \times 0.53 = 1.0017$.} The two statements are therefore, to 0.17\%, a
single one: the hydrogenic ionization energy divides between the two targets
in the ratio $n(\mathrm{H}) : 1.89\,n(\mathrm{H_2})$, with H$_2$ counted 1.89
times per molecule. \textbf{That identification is not made in the paper}; it
is read off here from the two published coefficients, and it is recorded as
ours both here and in \texttt{electron\_energy\_degradation.f90}.

It is worth having rather than being a curiosity. Written as two mean
energies, each expression divides by a density that vanishes at one end of
the composition range; written as the weight
%
\begin{equation*}
  u(r) = \frac{1.89\,n(\mathrm{H_2})}{n(\mathrm{H}) + 1.89\,n(\mathrm{H_2})},
\end{equation*}
%
the same physics is bounded in $[0,1]$, exact at both ends, and needs no
guard. It is also what makes the whole change collapse to nothing when
$n(\mathrm{H_2}) = 0$.

\textbf{Frelikh \& Murray-Clay (2026, ApJ 996, 96) weight by
$n(\mathrm{H_2})/[n(\mathrm{H}) + n(\mathrm{H_2})]$, citing Glassgold, Galli
\& Padovani (2012) eq.\ (11); read at the source, that equation is a statement
about a different quantity and is not a rival prescription for THIS split.}
Glassgold et al.'s eq.\ (11) is the dissociation heating per ion pair,
%
\begin{equation*}
  Q_{\rm diss} = \frac{x(\mathrm{H_2})}{x(\mathrm{H}) + x(\mathrm{H_2})}
                 \frac{D_0}{1 + C x_e^{\alpha}}, \qquad D_0 = 2.14\ \mathrm{eV},
\end{equation*}
%
one term of the heat budget of their eq.\ (3) and taken from Dalgarno et al.'s
Table 5; they apply the same plain number fraction to their vibrational
heating in eqs.\ (13) and (14). Frelikh \& Murray-Clay's eqs.\ (27), (28) and
(35) apply it to exactly those heating terms, so the attribution is accurate,
and neither paper restates the ionization-energy split of Dalgarno et al.'s
eqs.\ (9) and (10).

\textbf{Where the two weights do meet is the dissociation heat}, which
\texttt{photoelectron\_energy\_partition} also weights by $u$
(\texttt{f\_diss} and \texttt{f\_fluor}, the ``dissociation heat'' and
``heating amplitude'' subsections of this section). There the difference is real ---
$0.65$ against $0.50$ at $n(\mathrm{H_2})/n(\mathrm{H}) = 1$, and $0.159$
against $0.091$ at $0.1$ --- and we follow Dalgarno et al., whose Figure 20
states the dissociation yield as a number of dissociations \emph{per
$\mathrm{H_2^+}$ ion}: it tracks the $\mathrm{H_2^+}$ production that
eq.\ (10) weights, rather than the number fraction of molecules. Their own
eq.\ (11) is a third thing again --- the vibrational yield
$Y = Y_{\rm HeH_2}\, r/(r + a)$, which is what \texttt{f\_vib} uses.

\subsection*{The ionization channels}

\texttt{svs85\_secondary\_branching} already renormalized the H/He split onto
the cell's own neutral ratio, leaving the total ionization energy at the
Shull \& van Steenberg value. The generalization adds a third target to the
same construction, with H$_2$ entering the weight at 1.89 per molecule:
%
\begin{align*}
  n_{Hw} &= n_{\mathrm{H\,I}} + 1.89\,n_{\mathrm{H_2}}, \qquad
  w_{\rm tot} = n_{Hw}\,\eta_{\rm ref} f_{\mathrm{H\,I}}
              + n_{\mathrm{He\,I}} f_{\mathrm{He\,I}},\\
  c_{\mathrm{H\,I}} &= f_{\rm ion}\,\eta_{\rm ref}
              f_{\mathrm{H\,I}}/w_{\rm tot}, \qquad
  c_{\mathrm{H_2}} = 1.89\,c_{\mathrm{H\,I}}, \qquad
  c_{\mathrm{He\,I}} = f_{\rm ion}
              f_{\mathrm{He\,I}}/w_{\rm tot},
\end{align*}
%
with $\eta_{\rm ref} = 0.1$ the neutral He/H ratio the fits were measured at.
The construction conserves energy identically,
%
\begin{equation*}
  n_{\mathrm{H\,I}} c_{\mathrm{H\,I}}
  + n_{\mathrm{H_2}} c_{\mathrm{H_2}}
  + n_{\mathrm{He\,I}} c_{\mathrm{He\,I}} = f_{\rm ion},
\end{equation*}
%
for every composition. That is the property that makes it safe to move
energy between the channels: the H$_2$ channel is fed by taking from
H\,\textsc{i}, not by inventing.

\textbf{Checked against its source.} In a neutral, fully molecular gas the
construction implies a mean energy per H$_2^+$ ion of
$E_{\rm th}(\mathrm{H_2})/f_{\mathrm{H\,I}}(0) = 15.4/0.3908 =
39.4$~eV, against the $\mathbf{41.9}$~\textbf{eV} of Dalgarno et al.\
Table 4 (H$_2$ and He mixture, 1 keV). The 6\% is the same size as the
disagreement between the two sources' own mean energy per H$^+$ (Dalgarno et
al.\ section 6 quote 37.2 eV for Shull \& van Steenberg against their own
39.5 eV) and is well inside Dalgarno et al.'s stated 15\%.

An arithmetic aside, because it explains that 37.2 eV. Shull \& van
Steenberg's fitted amplitude gives $13.598/0.3908 = 34.8$~eV at $x = 0$, not
37.2. Their Monte Carlo at their lowest tabulated point, $x = 10^{-4}$, gives
$\phi(\mathrm{H\,I}) = 0.3656$, i.e.\ $13.598/0.3656 = 37.2$~eV
exactly. Dalgarno et al.\ quoted the \emph{data}, not the fit; the fit's
extrapolation to $x = 0$ overshoots its own Monte Carlo by 7\%.

The rate enters the chemistry through \texttt{P\_H2}, the channel that
already drives both the H$_2$ destruction row and the H$_2^+$ production row
of \texttt{System\_HeH\_mol} --- the same route the primary photoionization
takes --- so no parallel path was added.

\textbf{How much energy the new channel actually takes.} This is exact and
needs no run: the split is a function of the cell's neutral densities alone.
Evaluated on the composition of \texttt{mol\_base\_handoff}, as fractions of
the Shull \& van Steenberg ionization budget $f_{\rm ion}$:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lrrrr}
\toprule
$n(\mathrm{H_2})/n(\mathrm{H\,I})$ & H\,I & He\,I & \textbf{H$_2$} & sum$/f_{\rm ion}$ \\
\midrule
736         & 0.0006 & 0.1063 & \textbf{0.8930} & 1.0000000 \\
347         & 0.0014 & 0.1063 & \textbf{0.8923} & 1.0000000 \\
85          & 0.0056 & 0.1063 & \textbf{0.8881} & 1.0000000 \\
6.8         & 0.0648 & 0.1061 & \textbf{0.8291} & 1.0000000 \\
6.2 (base)  & 0.0705 & 0.1059 & \textbf{0.8236} & 1.0000000 \\
0.011 (top) & 0.8793 & 0.1024 & \textbf{0.0183} & 1.0000000 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\textbf{Through the molecular layer, 82--89\% of the secondary ionization
energy now goes to H$_2$ rather than to H\,I.} Before this change all of it
went to H\,I --- the docstring of the routine it replaces said so in as many
words. The last column is the energy identity holding to every printed digit
at every composition.


\subsection*{The dissociation heat, and where Frelikh's version overshoots}

Dalgarno et al.\ section 5.3 gives the kinetic energy released when H$_2$ is
dissociated through a triplet state as a mean of $\mathbf{5.4}$~\textbf{eV}
(``cannot be much different from a mean of 5.4 eV corresponding to a vertical
transition''). Frelikh \& Murray-Clay apply that 5.4 eV to the whole
\texttt{Dissociation} yield of Table 5. But that yield is the total, and its
footnote b says so: it excludes only the dissociative excitation channel, not
the singlet predissociation. The singlet route releases about 0.4 eV, not
5.4, and its share is fixed by the same paper --- section 5.3 gives radiative
dissociation probabilities of $\mathbf{0.27}$ for $B^1\Sigma_u^+$ and
$\mathbf{0.036}$ for $C^1\Pi_u$.

Separating the two reproduces the answer Dalgarno et al.\ state directly (the
dissociation heat per H$_2^+$ ion, 11 eV at 30 eV and 1.7 eV at 1 keV, their
sections 5.3 and 6) far better than not separating them:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
$E_0$ & Frelikh $5.4E/W_{\rm diss}$ & with the singlet split & Dalgarno's own value \\
\midrule
30 eV  &  4.67 eV & \textbf{4.31 eV} &  4.23 eV \\
1 keV  & 58.3 eV  & \textbf{45.4 eV} & 40.6 eV \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\noindent 10\% and 44\% against 2\% and 12\%. The split is what the code does.

The dissociation heat carries \textbf{no critical-density factor, and should
not}: the 5.4 eV and the 0.4 eV are translational from the moment they are
released. The vibrational and Lyman--Werner returns are internal excitation
and do need one; they are not in this change.

\subsection*{The seam between the two sources is an energy axis, not a
disagreement}

The H$_2$ target channel above was staged behind the heating amplitude, so
that the first step could be checked by bit-identity on the atomic cases. In
that step the heating fraction was carried as a \emph{ratio},
%
\begin{equation*}
  f_{\rm heat} = f_{\rm SvS85}(x)\,
     \frac{\eta_{\rm mix}(x,E_0,r)}{\eta_{\rm H,He}(x,E_0)}
     + u(r)\,f_{\rm diss}(x,E_0),
\end{equation*}
%
with $\eta_{\rm mix}$ from Dalgarno et al.\ eq.\ (12): the ratio keeps
Shull \& van Steenberg as the amplitude and is exactly 1 in a gas without
H$_2$. Repairing the amplitude, defect (3), is what this subsection decides
and the next one implements.

The first design considered was to use Dalgarno's $\eta$ below $x = 0.1$,
where his fits are stated, and Shull \& van Steenberg's above it, and to join
them. The offset at the join was measured before committing to that plan, and
it did not come out where it was expected to:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
$E_0$ & $\eta_{\rm Dalgarno}(0.1)$ & $f_{\rm SvS85}(0.1)$ & offset \\
\midrule
30 eV   & 0.9625 & 0.6400 & $+33.5$\% \\
50 eV   & 0.9078 & ''     & $+29.5$\% \\
100 eV  & 0.8384 & ''     & $+23.7$\% \\
200 eV  & 0.7749 & ''     & $+17.4$\% \\
500 eV  & 0.7075 & ''     & $+9.5$\% \\
1000 eV & 0.6691 & ''     & $+4.4$\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\textbf{Read as two determinations of one quantity that is a disagreement far
larger than either source's stated error. It is not one.} The footnote to
Shull \& van Steenberg's Table 1 says their fractional energy depositions are
``of a \textbf{3 keV} primary electron'', and their Figure 4, from which
Table 2 is fitted, is captioned ``Limiting values ($E_0 > 100$ eV)''. Their
fit is therefore a single high-energy asymptote with no $E_0$ axis at all,
while Dalgarno et al.'s Table 7 resolves $E_0$ and finds $\eta$ at $x = 0.1$
changing by 25\% between 100 eV and 1 keV --- $0.8384$ to $0.6691$. (The
44\% figure that stood here is the 30 eV to 1 keV range; 30 eV is outside the
$E_0 > 100$ eV range Shull \& van Steenberg claim, so it cannot be used to
argue against them. 25\% is enough, and it is the honest number.)
\textbf{The column above is not
two calculations disagreeing; it is one $E$-resolved calculation compared
against the other's 3 keV asymptote.} At the one energy where the two
describe the same thing --- Dalgarno's highest row, 1 keV --- the offset is
4.4\%, and Shull \& van Steenberg's own Monte Carlo at $x = 0.1$ is
$0.6524 \pm 0.0421$, which contains it.

The right test is therefore against the \emph{data} rather than against the
other fit. Judged on Shull \& van Steenberg's Table 1, over $x > 0.1$:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lrr}
\toprule
prescription & max relative deviation & max deviation / $1\sigma$ \\
\midrule
Shull \& van Steenberg's own fit          & 3.9\% ($x=0.2$) & 1.05 ($x=0.3$) \\
Dalgarno eq.\ (14) at 1 keV, extrapolated & 9.2\% ($x=0.95$) & 8.45 ($x=0.95$) \\
Dalgarno $+$ the neutral-fraction closure & 5.6\% ($x=0.15$) & 1.01 ($x=0.15$) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

and below $x = 0.1$ the Dalgarno branch stays within $0.90\sigma$ everywhere
while Shull \& van Steenberg's fit reaches $2.77\sigma$ at $x = 10^{-4}$ and
collapses below it. \textbf{The right design is therefore one expression over
the whole range: Dalgarno's $\eta$ everywhere, extrapolated above $x = 0.1$,
with a closure that supplies the $x = 1$ endpoint his fitting form does not
have.} It tracks Shull \& van Steenberg's own Monte Carlo about as well as
their fit does over the range where the fit was made, and much better outside
it.

\emph{A note on the third row.} It was first recorded as 6.8\% and
$1.89\sigma$, for a closure described in words but preserved neither in code
nor in a script. That closure could not be reconstructed, and the row now
carries the measurement of the closure actually implemented, which is the
better of the two on both measures. The first two rows are reproduced exactly
by re-evaluating the two published fits against Table 1.

\subsection*{The heating amplitude, and the closure that supplies the
endpoint}

\textbf{The judgement: Shull \& van Steenberg's heating fit is the wrong
function in a weakly ionized gas, and it is not a matter of degree.} Their
Form 1, $C[1 - (1 - x^a)^b]$, was chosen ``because of their appropriate
limits at $x = 0$ and $x = 1$'' --- and its $x = 0$ limit is \emph{zero}. A
neutral gas does not convert none of a photoelectron's energy to heat: it
converts $0.117$ of a 1 keV primary and $0.259$ of a 30 eV one (Dalgarno et
al.\ Table 7), and Shull \& van Steenberg's own Monte Carlo says
$0.1358 \pm 0.0088$ at their lowest tabulated point. In our molecular layer,
at $x = 10^{-16}$ to $5\times10^{-5}$, their fit was returning $0.1\%$ to
$1.5\%$.

The heating fraction is now Dalgarno et al.'s, at every $x$:
%
\begin{equation*}
  f_{\rm heat}(x, E_0) = 1 - \bigl[1 - \eta_{\rm mix}(x, E_0, r)\bigr](1-x)
     + f_{\rm diss} + f_{\rm vib} + f_{\rm fluor},
\end{equation*}
%
with $\eta_{\rm mix}$ their eq.\ (12). Shull \& van Steenberg's heating fit is
no longer called.

\textbf{The $(1-x)$ factor is a closure and is ours.} Dalgarno et al.\ state
eq.\ (14) ``for $x \leq 0.1$'', and its form leaves $(1-\eta_0)/(1+c)$ of the
primary energy unthermalized at $x = 1$ --- 10\% of it at 1 keV --- which is
impossible in a gas with no neutral left to ionize or excite. The factor says
that the channels competing with heat need a neutral to act on, so their
share must fall in proportion to the neutral fraction of the H and He nuclei,
which is exactly $1-x$ when $x$ is the electron density over those nuclei. It
has no free parameter, it is 1 to within $10^{-4}$ over the whole molecular
layer, and it forces $f_{\rm heat}(1) = 1$ exactly.

\textbf{What this does \emph{not} justify.} Evaluating eq.\ (14) above
$x = 0.1$ is extrapolation beyond the range its authors state, and forcing
the endpoint is not the same as the fit being right in between. The
extrapolation is accepted on a measurement instead, against Shull \& van
Steenberg's Table 1 --- their Monte Carlo, 18 points with $1\sigma$ widths,
not their fit:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{rrrrrrrrr}
\toprule
$x$ & Table 1 & $1\sigma$ & SvS85 fit & dev & $\eta_D$(1 keV) & dev & closed & dev \\
\midrule

0.90 & 0.9847 & 0.0123 & 0.9882 & $+0.4\%$ & 0.8949 & $-9.1\%$ & 0.9895 & $+0.5\%$ \\

(``closed'' is the prescription now in the code, at Dalgarno's 1 keV row ---
his highest, since Table 1 is a 3 keV calculation.) Over $x > 0.1$ the
closure is $5.6\%$ and $1.01\sigma$ at worst against $3.9\%$ and $1.05\sigma$
for Shull \& van Steenberg's own fit; over $x \leq 0.1$ it is $11.3\%$ and
$1.40\sigma$ against their $18.0\%$ and $2.77\sigma$, and their fit keeps
falling below that while ours does not. \textbf{There is no seam}: one
expression covers the whole domain, so the question of where to join the two
sources does not arise.

\textbf{Measured} on the two converged cases that fire the coupling
(\texttt{wasp\_full\_newton}, \texttt{wasp\_he23off\_newton}): escaping mass
flux $+3.6\%$, $\log_{10}\dot M$ 13.20 to 13.22, photoheating $+22\%$ at
$r = 1.075$ and the temperature $+9\%$ at $r = 1.086$, and under $0.5\%$
above $r = 1.6$ where $x$ is already 0.99.

\subsection*{\texttt{E\_sec\_ion}: 40 eV was another code's number}

\texttt{E\_sec\_ion} is the photoelectron energy above which the partition is
applied at all. It was 40 eV, and the code site said where that came from:
``matching the wind\_ae X-ray cutoff''. That is a numerical convention of a
different code, not a physical threshold, and it sat between the two sources
rather than on either.

It is now \textbf{30 eV}, the lowest primary energy at which any coefficient
of the partition is \emph{published} --- Dalgarno et al.\ tabulate 30, 50,
100, 200, 500 and 1000 eV. What is still discarded is written at the code
site: a $13.6$--$30$ eV photoelectron can ionize hydrogen, and in the
hot-Uranus band those photons carry 18\% of the incident XUV energy, but no
source consulted resolves the partition there.

\textbf{Measured}, on its own build: escaping mass flux $-0.17\%$ and
$-0.13\%$, $\log_{10}\dot M$ unchanged at 13.22, photoheating $-1.6\%$ at
$r = 1.3$. The sign is right --- those photoelectrons now spend part of their
energy ionizing instead of all of it heating --- and the size is what
\texttt{TO\_BE\_DONE.md} (P32) predicted.

\subsection*{The ionization channels get the energy axis they were missing}

Shull \& van Steenberg's $\phi(\mathrm{H\,\textsc{i}})$ and
$\phi(\mathrm{He\,\textsc{i}})$ have no $E_0$ dependence: their Table 2
footnote says ``These formulae are only accurate for $E_0 > 100$ eV'' and
Table 1 is a 3 keV calculation. Dalgarno et al.'s Table 4 supplies what is
missing, so the amplitude is now theirs in $E$ and Shull \& van Steenberg's
in $x$:
%
\begin{align*}
  f_{\mathrm{H\,\textsc{i}}}(x,E_0)  &= \phi_{\mathrm{H\,\textsc{i}}}(x)\,
      W_{\mathrm{H^+}}(x, 1\,\mathrm{keV}) / W_{\mathrm{H^+}}(x, E_0), \\
  f_{\mathrm{He\,\textsc{i}}}(x,E_0) &= \phi_{\mathrm{He\,\textsc{i}}}(x)\,
      W_{\mathrm{He^+}}(x, 1\,\mathrm{keV}) / W_{\mathrm{He^+}}(x, E_0).
\end{align*}
%
\textbf{The ratio is 1 at the top of the table}, so the high-energy limit is
exactly Shull \& van Steenberg's. Below it a photoelectron makes fewer ion
pairs per unit energy, and for helium the effect is large:
$W_{\mathrm{He^+}}$ rises from 487 eV at 1 keV to 6740 eV at 30 eV, so a
30 eV photoelectron puts 14 times less of its energy into
He\,\textsc{i} ionization than the unresolved fit asserts --- which is
physical, 30 eV being barely above helium's 24.6 eV threshold. For hydrogen
the factor is 1.51. The collision weight 1.89 is deliberately \emph{not}
given an energy dependence: Dalgarno et al.\ state their eqs.\ (9) and (10)
coefficients once, not per energy.

\textbf{Plumbing.} $E_0 = h\nu - E_{\rm th}$ depends only on the spectral bin
and the absorber's own threshold, both fixed for a run, so the bracket index
and interpolation weight are built once at startup
(\texttt{photoelectron\_energy\_grid}, called from
\texttt{set\_energy\_vectors}) and each cell then costs one gather and one
linear interpolation per bin. Without that, the heating-amplitude change
alone cost 49\% in run time (3\,m\,40\,s to 5\,m\,27\,s on
\texttt{wasp\_full\_newton}); with it the same case runs in 3\,m\,51\,s,
5\% above the original while doing strictly more work.

\textbf{Measured}: escaping mass flux $+0.64\%$ and $+0.53\%$,
$\log_{10}\dot M$ unchanged, temperature $+3.8\%$ at $r = 1.13$, photoheating
$+3.3\%$ to $+5.2\%$ at $r = 1.25$, and $n(\mathrm{H^+})/n(\mathrm H)$ down
13\% at $r = 1.10$ --- the weakly ionized shell fed by the softest
photoelectrons.

\subsection*{\texttt{xion} was not the electron fraction}

Dalgarno et al.\ section 7 defines the ionization fraction of the
H-H$_2$-He mixture as ``the number density ratio of the electrons to the
hydrogen and helium nuclei''. EXHALE built it at three sites ---
\texttt{ionization\_equilibrium.f90}, \texttt{util\_ion\_eq.f90},
\texttt{post\_process\_adv.f90} --- as
$(n_{\mathrm{H^+}} + n_{\mathrm{He^+}} + n_{\mathrm{He^{2+}}})/
(n_{\mathrm H} + n_{\mathrm{He}})$, a count of H and He \emph{ions}: it
omitted every molecular-ion electron and every metal electron, and counted
He\,\textsc{iii} once although it releases two. In the metals-on molecular
gate the two differ by up to nine decades.

The numerator is now the total free-electron density, \texttt{calc\_ne}'s own
value; the denominator stays the nuclei. \textbf{The metal electrons are an
extension beyond both sources' composition} and are marked as such at the
code site: neither Monte Carlo had a metal in it, and the reason for
including them anyway is that what degrades a photoelectron is Coulomb
scattering off free electrons, which an electron released by a metal does as
well as one released by hydrogen. It also lets the ratio exceed one, which is
why every entry point clamps into $[0,1]$. One asymmetry is recorded rather
than removed: on the post-process path the molecular-ion electrons are still
absent, because that path does not carry the molecular densities at all.

\textbf{Measured}: escaping mass flux $+0.94\%$ and $+0.81\%$,
$\log_{10}\dot M$ unchanged, photoheating $+8.6\%$ at the base itself
($r = 1.000$) and the base temperature $+2.1\%$ at $r = 1.02$ --- where the
metal electrons dominate the free-electron budget of the shielded gas.

\subsection*{The two heat returns that were blocked on constants, and their
sources}

\textbf{What Dalgarno et al.'s heating efficiency is \emph{not}.} Their
section 5.3 defines it as ``the heating efficiency, defined as the fraction
of the primary energy that is converted into heat from elastic scattering and
rotational excitations''. Vibrational excitation is outside it, explicitly:
``The fraction of the energy $E$ lost in vibrational excitation is
illustrated in Figure 11. If the vibrationally excited H$_2$ radiates the
excitation energy is lost. However, if it is collisionally quenched, the
excitation energy is converted into heat.''

\textbf{(a) Direct vibrational excitation, $v = 1$ and $v = 2$.} Table 5's
own rows for those levels give the mean energy per excitation in the
H$_2$-He mixture; the level energies are the Roueff et al.\ (2019) term
values the code already carries for the infrared lines, $0.51592$~eV for
$(v{=}1,J{=}0)$ and $\mathbf{1.00266}$~eV for $(v{=}2,J{=}0)$ --- not the
harmonic twice-$0.516$, which is 2.8\% high. The yield is transferred to a
mixture containing atomic hydrogen by eqs.\ (11), (16) and (17), which are
one expression, $Y = Y_{\rm HeH_2}\,r/(r+a)$ with $r = n(\mathrm{H_2})/n(\mathrm H)$.

\emph{A typographical correction, made and stated.} The paper prints
$a(x) = 0.5 \times (x/10^{4})^{0.15}$ for the middle range. With the exponent
as printed, eq.\ (17) gives $a = 0.0316$ at $x = 10^{-4}$ where eq.\ (16)
requires $0.5$, and $a = 0.0112$ at $x = 10^{-7}$ where eq.\ (11) requires
$0.177$ --- two discontinuities, \textbf{both by the same factor 15.85}. With
$10^{-4}$ in place of $10^{4}$ the expression meets eq.\ (16) exactly at
$x = 10^{-4}$ and eq.\ (11) to three digits at $x = 10^{-7}$ ($0.1774$
against their $0.177$). Since $15.85 = (10^{8})^{0.15}$ is exactly the ratio
between the two readings, the sign of the exponent is the whole discrepancy,
and the minus sign is taken to have been lost in typesetting.

\textbf{(b) The fluorescence return.} Of the B and C excitations, $0.27$ and
$0.036$ dissociate; the rest fluoresce back into \emph{bound}, vibrationally
excited levels of the ground state. Black \& van Dishoeck (1987),
pp.~412--413: ``The initial absorptions are followed by fluorescence to the
vibrational continuum of the ground state with a typical average probability
of 0.10. \dots\ The remaining 90\% of the fluorescent transitions populate
various bound excited vibration-rotation levels of the ground state.'' The
energy left behind per pump is \textbf{2.0 eV}, from Burton, Hollenbach \&
Tielens (1990), Appendix A, p.~635: ``The process is approximated as per
Paper I, except that the effective heating per pump, $E_*$, has been taken as
2.0 eV.'' Their eq.\ (1) prefactor $3.2\times10^{-12}$ erg is exactly that.

Two limits are recorded with it. It is an \emph{adopted} value in Burton et
al., revised from their Paper I without a derivation; and \textbf{Black \&
van Dishoeck do not state it}, contrary to how it is usually attributed ---
what they supply is the branching above and a line-by-line intensity table.
Applying it to \emph{electron-impact} excitation of B and C, as well as to
photon pumping, is a further assumption: the upper states and the cascade are
the same, the distribution over upper vibrational levels is not.

\textbf{(c) The collisional-quench fraction.} Hollenbach \& McKee (1979),
p.~586: ``The term $(1 + n_{\rm cr}/n)^{-1}$ expresses the fraction of the
excitation energy going into heat via collisional de-excitation rather than
into radiation.'' $n_{\rm cr} = A/\gamma$ (their p.~576) with
$A_{10} = 8.3\times10^{-7}$~s$^{-1}$ (p.~583, $J$-averaged, from Turner,
Kirby-Docken \& Dalgarno 1977) and the rate coefficients of their eq.~(6.29).
The code carries it as $f = q/(q + A_{10})$ with
$q = \gamma_{\rm H} n_{\rm H\,\textsc{i}} + \gamma_{\rm H_2} n_{\rm H_2}$, in
\texttt{h2\_vibrational\_relaxation.f90} --- one file, so the two drivers
cannot drift apart.

\textbf{Note the direction: this factor is not a suppression.} It is the
statement that at high density the excitation energy \emph{does} become heat.
In our layer it is $1.0000$ to four digits everywhere, because
$n_{\rm cr}(v{=}1)$ is $5.0\times10^{4}$~cm$^{-3}$ against atomic H and
$1.1\times10^{6}$~cm$^{-3}$ against H$_2$ at $950$--$1300$~K, while the layer
carries $n(\mathrm{H_2}) = 4.4\times10^{9}$ to $4.6\times10^{13}$~cm$^{-3}$.
It is written out anyway, because a shallower base would not be.

\emph{This also fixes an uncited number elsewhere in the tree.} Both
\texttt{molecular\_infrared\_\allowbreak cooling.f90} and
\texttt{molecular\_hydrogen\_\allowbreak treatment.tex} used
``$n_{\rm crit}(\mathrm{H_2}\,v{=}1) \sim 10^{9}$--$10^{11}$~cm$^{-3}$'' as a
validity argument for LTE level populations, with no citation. Evaluated from
Hollenbach \& McKee it is $2$--$6\times10^{6}$~cm$^{-3}$ (H$_2$ collider) or
$5$--$8\times10^{4}$~cm$^{-3}$ (H collider) over $900$--$1350$~K --- three to
five decades lower, which \emph{widens} the LTE margin. Both sites now carry
the sourced value. Neither source gives a \textbf{helium} collision rate for
H$_2$ $v=1$, so a helium-dominated gas is outside both; helium is left out of
the collider sum rather than given a borrowed rate, which errs towards
radiating the energy away rather than towards claiming it as heat.

\textbf{How large the two returns are}, exactly and needing no run, on the
\texttt{mol\_base\_handoff} layer:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
 & base & mid-layer & top \\
\midrule
$n(\mathrm{H_2})/n(\mathrm{H\,\textsc{i}})$ & 6.2 & 31 & 0.011 \\
$f_{\rm heat}$ at 30 eV, without (a) and (b) & 0.235 & 0.244 & 0.264 \\
$f_{\rm heat}$ at 30 eV, with them & \textbf{0.394} & \textbf{0.407} & 0.265 \\
$f_{\rm heat}$ at 1 keV, without (a) and (b) & 0.098 & 0.103 & 0.125 \\
$f_{\rm heat}$ at 1 keV, with them & \textbf{0.196} & \textbf{0.204} & 0.126 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\textbf{The two returns roughly double the molecular heat fraction}, and they
vanish where the H$_2$ does, as they must.

\textbf{(d) The photon-driven half of the same physics.}
\texttt{lyman\_werner.f90} already knew that only 13.5\% of Lyman--Werner
pumps dissociate, and \texttt{ionization\_equilibrium.f90} deposited the
0.4 eV those dissociations give the fragment pair. The other 86.5\% were
accounted as energy that does not come back. At the density of a molecular
base that is wrong, and the missing term is
$(k_{\rm LW}/p_{\rm diss})(1-p_{\rm diss})\,n(\mathrm{H_2})\,E_*\,f_{\rm q}$,
whose prefactor is $(0.865/0.135)\times(2.0/0.4) = 32$ times the fragment
term that was there. It uses the same two constants from the same file as the
electron-driven channel.

\textbf{And it is not a correction, it is the channel.} Measured on
\texttt{mol\_lyman\_werner}, the only default case that carries a stellar
Lyman--Werner field, from its own \texttt{Heating\_breakdown.txt}:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lr}
\toprule
 & value \\
\midrule
Lyman--Werner heating at the base cell & $1.216\times10^{-8}$ erg cm$^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$ \\
total photoheating at the base cell & $2.492\times10^{-8}$ erg cm$^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$ \\
\textbf{Lyman--Werner share at the base} & \textbf{48.8\%} \\
Lyman--Werner share over $r = 1.0$--$1.2$ & 66.2\% \\
peak Lyman--Werner heating & $3.568\times10^{-8}$ at $r = 1.078$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

With only the 0.4 eV fragment term the same cell would carry
$3.685\times10^{-10}$ in that channel and a total of $1.313\times10^{-8}$:
\textbf{the base photoheating of a molecular layer under a Lyman--Werner
field was low by a factor of 1.9.} The column-integrated FUV ledger of
\texttt{write\_output.f90} moves with it --- the 86.5\% of pumped photon
energy it used to book as \texttt{bond\_col}, energy that never returns, is
now the largest single heating term of the layer --- and the run's mean
photoheating over $r < 1.2$ rises 20.5\% once the wind relaxes to it.
(\texttt{mol\_lyman\_werner} is a 12000-step snapshot, so that last number is
a direction and an order, not a converged answer.)

\subsection*{What is still not here}

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Dissociative ionization of H$_2$}, for which Dalgarno et al.\
  give a mean energy of $22\,W_m(\mathrm{H_2^+})$: about 4.5\% of the H$_2$
  ionizations. It was absent from the primary photoionization as well.
  \textbf{Both sides are now carried; see Sec.~\ref{sec:h2-dissoc-photoion}},
  which also corrects the branching the primary side would have used.
\item \textbf{The Ly$\alpha$ excitation channel}, still treated as escaping
  line radiation rather than coupled to the Ly$\alpha$ field of the
  excited-hydrogen model.
\item \textbf{Electrons as a collider} for the H$_2$ vibrational quench:
  Burton et al.'s Table 7 gives an $e$-H$_2$ rate about two orders above the
  H$_2$-H$_2$ one, but the molecular layer runs at an electron fraction of
  $10^{-16}$ to $5\times10^{-5}$.
\item \textbf{A helium-dominated gas.} Neither degradation source samples
  one, and neither vibrational-quench source gives a helium rate. This is the
  validity limit that matters most for the He/H $= 1$--$10$ cases, and it is
  in the header of both new modules.
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Structure and verification}

Two names were corrected before anything else was touched, and the rename
alone was verified byte-identical on all eight regression cases:
\texttt{photoelectron\_partition\_cell} became
\texttt{photoelectron\_energy\_partition} (\texttt{\_cell} names a place in
the code, not a physical quantity), and \texttt{dal\_eta\_node} /
\texttt{dal\_W\_node} became \texttt{dalgarno\_heating\_efficiency} /
\texttt{dalgarno\_mean\_energy\_per\_ion\_pair}.

\texttt{svs85\_secondary\_branching} computed a partition blind to both the
molecular content and the photoelectron energy, and its name named a source
rather than a physical quantity. It is replaced by
\texttt{src/modules/radiation/electron\_energy\_degradation.f90}, holding
both sources' fits and three entry points:
\texttt{photoelectron\_energy\_grid} (once at startup),
\texttt{photoelectron\_energy\_partition} (once per cell) and
\texttt{photoelectron\_shares} (once per absorber). The leaf functions keep
their source names (\texttt{svs85\_fion\_HI}, \ldots) in the convention
\texttt{rr\_badnell} and \texttt{h2\_self\_shielding\_richings} already set.
\texttt{h2\_vibrational\_relaxation.f90} holds the two constants and the
quench fraction the electron-driven and photon-driven channels share.

The split into a per-cell part and a per-energy part is what keeps the cost
down: the powers $x^a$ are evaluated once per cell at the six tabulated
energies, and each absorber then costs one gather and one interpolation per
spectral bin, on \emph{its own} excess energy $h\nu - E_{\rm th}$ rather than
a single shared one, with the bracket and weight built once at startup.

\textbf{Verification.}
\begin{itemize}
\item The module was compiled standalone against an independent Python
  implementation of the same equations and agrees \textbf{to every printed
  digit} over 24 combinations of ionized fraction ($0$, $10^{-8}$,
  $10^{-5}$, $10^{-2}$) and $n(\mathrm{H_2})/n(\mathrm{H})$ ($0$, $0.1$,
  $1$, $10^3$) at all six tabulated energies. Re-run after each of the four
  changes.
\item Energy conservation,
  $n_{\mathrm{H\,I}} c_{\mathrm{H\,I}} +
   n_{\mathrm{H_2}} c_{\mathrm{H_2}} +
   n_{\mathrm{He\,I}} c_{\mathrm{He\,I}} = f_{\rm ion}$,
  holds \textbf{exactly} at every one of those points and at every tabulated
  energy.
\item At 1 keV and $n(\mathrm{H_2}) = 0$ the partition reduces to Shull \&
  van Steenberg's own per-atom values, $c_{\mathrm{H\,I}} = 0.3908$ and
  $c_{\mathrm{He\,I}} = 0.554$ at
  $n(\mathrm{He\,\textsc{i}})/n(\mathrm{H\,\textsc{i}}) = 0.1$ --- the check
  that the energy ratios are normalized where they should be.
\item The vibrational and fluorescence channels leave the two converged
  atomic cases \textbf{byte-identical}, which is the evidence that the
  H$_2$ terms are zero when they should be rather than merely small.
\item Rebuilt with \texttt{-fcheck=bounds,do,mem} and run bounded on three
  cases --- HD\,209458\,b (1500 steps), \texttt{mol\_sec\_ion} and
  \texttt{mol\_lyman\_werner} (800 each, so that both new molecular paths
  are entered) --- with \textbf{no trap}. That matters here because the
  interpolation table \texttt{sec\_kE}/\texttt{sec\_wE} is indexed by an
  absorber number that runs past the five fixed edges into the metal ions.
\item \texttt{make check} on the refreshed goldens is \textbf{byte-identical
  on all nine cases}, re-run once more after the optimized rebuild that
  followed the runtime-checked one.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{And the molecular gates could not test any of it, which is a finding
in its own right.} \texttt{Secondary\_ionization} defaults to \textsc{staged}:
the coupling is switched on only after the wind first converges without it.
Every molecular regression case is a fixed-\texttt{maxsteps} relaxation
snapshot that never converges --- \texttt{mol\_base\_handoff} ends at
$du = 2.48$ --- so \texttt{sec\_ion\_active} never flips, \texttt{sec\_on} is
false for the whole run, and the entire partition path, old and new, is
bypassed. A sweep of every case's \texttt{run.log} found the line ``secondary
ionization activated'' in exactly four: \texttt{wasp\_full},
\texttt{wasp\_full\_newton}, \texttt{wasp\_he23off},
\texttt{wasp\_he23off\_newton}. None of the molecular gates, and not
\texttt{lower\_profile}.

So a molecular gate coming back byte-identical under a change to this physics
is \textbf{not} evidence that the change is small. It is evidence that the
channel is switched off in that case, and that \textbf{the regression matrix
had never exercised secondary ionization in a molecular gas at all}.

\textbf{\texttt{mol\_sec\_ion} closes that hole and is now a default case.}
It is \texttt{mol\_base\_handoff} with
\texttt{Secondary\_ionization: Immediate} and nothing else changed, at the
same 12000 steps, so it isolates the switch. It is the only case in the
matrix in which a photoelectron is partitioned in molecular gas, and it is
what guards the H$_2$ target, the dissociation heat and the two vibrational
returns. It was recorded as (P28) in \texttt{TO\_BE\_DONE.md}, which this
closes.

Two consequences for how the rest of this section reads. \textbf{Quantitative
movement is quoted only from \texttt{wasp\_full\_newton} and
\texttt{wasp\_he23off\_newton}}, the two converged cases in which the
coupling actually fires; the molecular gates are relaxation snapshots and are
used only for bit-identity and for the sign and order of a change. And every
``measured'' line above comes from its own build: the four changes were made
and measured one at a time, because all four move the same integral.

\textbf{A case that does exercise the path.} \texttt{mol\_base\_handoff} was
re-run with \texttt{Secondary\_ionization: Immediate} added and nothing else
changed, at the same 12000 steps, so the comparison is the switch and not the
code version. (This A/B was taken on the code with the H$_2$ target in and
the three later repairs not yet made; \texttt{mol\_sec\_ion} on the finished
code ends at $du = 2.46$, the same order again.) It completes with no NaN: $du$ rises through a transient peak
near step 2900 and relaxes back to 2.56 at step 12000, against 2.48 for the
staged run, i.e.\ to the same order. \textbf{Both are relaxation snapshots,
not converged solutions, and nothing quantitative should be read off them}
--- what they establish is that the path is live and stable, and the
direction:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lrr}
\toprule
 & secondary off (staged) & secondary on \\
\midrule
max $n_e/n_{\rm H}$ in the molecular layer & $5.0\times10^{-5}$ & $9.7\times10^{-5}$ \\
peak $n(\mathrm{H_3^+})$ [cm$^{-3}$] & $6.69\times10^{4}$ at $r = 1.032$ & $2.84\times10^{5}$ at $r = 1.016$ \\
H$_2$ front, $f(\mathrm{H_2}) = 0.5$ & $r = 1.158$ & $r = 1.143$ \\
layer temperature range [K] & 873--1309 & 905--1304 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The electron fraction roughly doubles and H$_3^+$ rises rather than falls.
\textbf{That is the opposite of the direction Frelikh \& Murray-Clay report},
where the extra electrons destroy H$_3^+$ faster than it forms. The two are
consistent if the difference is the weighting: our H$_2$ channel takes
82--89\% of the ionization energy in this layer and feeds H$_2^+$, which
converts to H$_3^+$ through R8, while their Glassgold weighting gives H$_2$
about half that share. Whether that is the whole explanation is not settled
here, and the comparison it belongs to is (P23), which requires a converged
solution.

\subsection*{The whole block, end to end}

Four changes, each built and measured on its own, on the two converged cases
that fire the coupling. Escaping mass flux $\rho v r^2$ at the escape radius,
\texttt{wasp\_full\_newton}:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lrrl}
\toprule
step & mass flux & $\log_{10}\dot M$ & largest local change \\
\midrule
starting point (rename only, byte-identical) & $6.3388\times10^{15}$ & 13.20 & --- \\
heating amplitude $+$ closure & $6.5682\times10^{15}$ ($+3.62\%$) & 13.22 & heat $+22\%$ at $r = 1.075$ \\
\texttt{E\_sec\_ion} $40 \to 30$ eV & $6.5567\times10^{15}$ ($-0.17\%$) & 13.22 & heat $-1.6\%$ at $r = 1.31$ \\
ionization channels resolved in $E_0$ & $6.5986\times10^{15}$ ($+0.64\%$) & 13.22 & $T$ $+3.8\%$ at $r = 1.13$ \\
\texttt{xion} $=$ electron fraction & $6.6604\times10^{15}$ ($+0.94\%$) & 13.22 & heat $+8.6\%$ at $r = 1.000$ \\
vibrational and fluorescence returns & $6.6604\times10^{15}$ ($0.00\%$) & 13.22 & byte-identical (no H$_2$) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\textbf{Cumulative: $+5.07\%$ in the escaping mass flux, $+0.02$ dex in
$\log_{10}\dot M$}, with \texttt{wasp\_he23off\_newton} giving $+4.91\%$ and
the same 13.20 to 13.22. The mass flux moves by five percent while the
reported $\dot M$ moves by two hundredths of a dex, which is the usual
reminder that a two-decimal $\dot M$ is not the quantity to judge a change
by.

The signature is where the changes land, not their size in the total: every
one of them is concentrated between $r = 1.0$ and $r = 1.3$, the weakly
ionized shell just above the base, and every one is under half a percent
above $r = 1.6$ where $x$ is already 0.99. That is the region where Shull \&
van Steenberg's fit was being evaluated eight to twelve decades outside its
stated range, and it is the region the molecular layer sits in.

\textbf{The regression matrix, and what its pass/fail pattern proves.} The
goldens were refreshed once, at the end of the block, with the previous set
preserved in \texttt{backup/regression/golden\_blockL\_20260902/}. Which
cases moved is itself the evidence for (P28):

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
case & verdict & why \\
\midrule
\texttt{wasp\_full} & moved & fires the coupling; $\dot M$ 13.23 to 13.26, 14091 to 11590 steps \\
\texttt{wasp\_he23off} & moved & fires the coupling; $\dot M$ 13.23 to 13.26, 14068 to 11269 steps \\
\texttt{mol\_lyman\_werner} & moved & carries a stellar Lyman--Werner field \\
\texttt{mol\_sec\_ion} & new & the only case that partitions in molecular gas \\
\texttt{mol\_base\_handoff} & \textbf{byte-identical} & staged coupling never fires, no LW field \\
\texttt{mol\_metals} & \textbf{byte-identical} & same \\
\texttt{mol\_diffusion} & \textbf{byte-identical} & same \\

\texttt{lower\_profile} & \textbf{byte-identical} & same \\
